# The Lantern on the River

The ferryman Zhao Mingzhi had crossed the Yellow River for forty years, and in all that time he had learned to read the water the way other men read faces. He knew when the current meant to drown a man, and he knew when it merely wanted to inconvenience him. He knew the sounds the river made at midnight, the particular gurgling beneath the dock, the way the reeds whispered when no wind was blowing.

He thought he knew everything about this stretch of water.

He was wrong.

---

It was the seventh month, the time when the gates of the underworld swing open and the hungry dead are permitted to wander among the living. Every household in the village had set out paper offerings and burning incense. Children were forbidden from going near the water after dark. Old women tied red string around their wrists and muttered sutras under their breath.

Zhao Mingzhi paid little attention to such customs. He was a practical man—a man of calluses and rope burns, of early mornings and fish-smelling clothes. The dead, he believed, were simply the absent. They had gone somewhere else, as travelers go somewhere else. That was the whole of it.

His wife had told him this attitude would bring trouble.

She had been dead for three years, so he no longer had to listen to her.

---

The night it began was ordinary in every way except one.

Zhao Mingzhi was preparing to tie off his boat and retire to his small house on the eastern bank when he saw the light. It floated on the far side of the river, perhaps twenty yards from shore—a pale lantern glow, amber and wavering, sitting perfectly still on the dark water.

He squinted at it. Fishermen sometimes used lanterns at night, but no fisherman let his craft sit motionless in the middle of the channel. The current would carry it downstream within seconds.

Yet this light did not move.

He watched it for a long while, scratching the back of his neck, reasoning with himself. A lantern caught on a sandbar, perhaps. A trick of the moonlight. He was sixty-three years old and his eyes were no longer the sharp instruments they had once been.

He went inside and slept without difficulty.

---

The light was there the following night as well, in precisely the same position.

And the night after that.

On the fourth evening, the miller's son came running down to the dock with a message from a merchant in Linfen who required urgent transport across the river at first light. The boy was twelve or thirteen, bright-eyed, with mud on both elbows. He delivered his message and then stood staring out at the water.

"What is that light?" he asked.

Zhao Mingzhi felt a coldness pass through him that had nothing to do with the autumn air. He had almost convinced himself the lantern was his own invention, born of old eyes and solitary evenings.

"Go home," he told the boy. "Don't look at it."

"Why? What is it?"

"Go home."

The boy went, glancing backward twice.

---

That night Zhao Mingzhi could not sleep. He lay on his mat and listened to the river and tried to remember everything his wife had told him about the hungry ghost festival—everything he had refused to properly hear while she was alive to say it.

The dead who had not been properly mourned, she had explained, were the dangerous ones. Those who had drowned, particularly. They could not enter the underworld until they found a substitute—another soul to take their place in the cold water. Until then they wandered the river's edge, patient as stones, wearing their death like a lantern to draw the living close.

*You set out offerings,* she had told him every year, arranging paper boats and spirit money on the water's surface. *You acknowledge them. You say: I see you, I remember you, go in peace. And they go.*

He had stood beside her while she did this, holding the incense, feeling faintly embarrassed by what he privately considered superstition.

He thought about that now, alone in the dark.

---

On the fifth night, he took his boat out.

He told himself he was being rational. He would row to where the light was, discover the mundane explanation—a jar of oil caught in some underwater growth, a reflection from the opposite bank—and the matter would be settled. He was a ferryman. The river was his occupation. He would not be chased from his own water by a light.

He rowed steadily, not looking up until he judged himself to be halfway across.

Then he looked.

The lantern was perhaps ten yards ahead of him, hovering just above the surface—and he could see now that it was not resting on anything. No boat beneath it. No pole supporting it. It simply existed, suspended, the flame inside it burning without any visible source.

And around it, illuminated by its pale glow, the river was wrong.

The water beneath the lantern was perfectly still. Not calm—still in the way that stone is still, or ice. The current moved on either side of it, he could see the black water sliding past, but in that small circle of light everything had stopped.

He stopped rowing.

The lantern turned.

He understood immediately, in the wordless way one understands things in dreams, that the lantern did not rotate. Rather, his perception of it shifted, as though it had a face that had been turned away from him and had now decided to look at him instead.

The cold he felt was profound and total. He was cold in his teeth, in the roots of his hair.

A voice came from the direction of the light. It was thin and strained, the voice of something speaking through a great distance or a great weight.

*"Ferryman,"* it said.

He could not speak. His tongue had become a stone in his mouth.

*"Ferryman, I have been waiting."*

"Who—" His voice cracked. He tried again. "Who are you?"

A pause. The river rushed past on both sides of that terrible stillness.

*"I don't remember,"* the voice said, and something about those three words—the bewildered honesty of them—broke through his fear and struck him somewhere deeper, somewhere more human. *"I have been here a long time. I was crossing. There was a storm."*

"When?" he managed. "When did you cross?"

*"I don't remember that either. There was a wife. Children, I think. I can't see their faces anymore."*

Zhao Mingzhi's hands were shaking. His oar rested loose in its lock. He thought about his own wife, the way her face had come to him less clearly in the three years since her death—how he sometimes reached for the precise color of her eyes and found only approximation.

"What do you want?" he asked.

The lantern flickered. When the voice returned it was somehow both closer and farther away, as if proximity meant nothing here.

*"I want to be remembered. Someone must remember me or I cannot leave. That is the rule. Someone must say: you existed. Someone must say: you mattered. Otherwise—"* The flame shuddered. *"Otherwise I stay. I stay and I am so cold, ferryman. The water is so cold here."*

He sat for a long moment in his rocking boat, on the dark river, in the seventh month when the gates are open, looking at a light that had no business existing.

Then he set down his oar.

"I don't know your name," he said. "I don't know your face. I don't know if you were a good man or a foolish one or something in between." He paused. "But you crossed this river once, and the river took you, and that is a terrible thing to happen to any person. You had a wife. You had children. You were trying to get home." His voice had gone rough. He was not, he realized, thinking only about the ghost. "You existed. You mattered. I, Zhao Mingzhi, ferryman of the Yellow River, say so. And I ask that you rest now. I ask that you go."

The silence that followed was the loudest he had ever heard.

Then, slowly, like a coal losing its heat, the lantern dimmed.

The still circle of water began to tremble, to move, to rejoin the current that had been flowing around it.

*"Thank you,"* said the voice, from a much greater distance.

And then there was only the river, and the darkness, and an ordinary night.

---

Zhao Mingzhi sat in his boat for a long time before he trusted himself to row back.

When he reached his dock and tied off and walked up to his small house, he did not go inside immediately. He stood at the water's edge and looked out at the current. Then he reached into his pocket and removed a stick of incense he had purchased in the village and never burned—had carried around for months, he realized, without knowing exactly why.

He lit it from his lamp. He set it upright in the soft earth of the bank.

"I remember you too," he said quietly, to the river and the night and whoever else might be listening. "You had very particular opinions about ghost month. You were right about that. You were right about a number of things." He watched the incense smoke curl upward and disperse. "I'm sorry it took me this long to say so."

The river offered no response, which was appropriate.

The living do not require voices from the dark to answer them.

Only the dead need that.

---

He crossed the Yellow River for seventeen more years, and in all that time he never saw the lantern again. Every seventh month, without fail, he set out paper offerings and burned incense and spoke a few quiet words to the empty air above the water.

His apprentices thought he was sentimental.

They did not understand that he was being precise.

There is a difference between remembering the dead and merely grieving them. Grief turns inward. Remembrance looks outward, toward whoever is being remembered—acknowledges them, returns them briefly to the world of the living, gives them the only gift the living can still give.

Zhao Mingzhi had learned this from a light on the water.

He had learned it from a man whose name he never knew.

He thought about that often, in his later years, rowing back and forth across the same brown river in all weathers—how much we carry that belongs to strangers. How much of what shapes us arrives without introduction, without context, bearing only the bare fact of itself.

A lantern. A voice. Three words spoken across dark water.

*I don't remember.*

He remembered enough for both of them.
